questions.q: Why does forcing an open-ended research question into a standard two-week sprint with story points tend to produce bad outcomes?
options: Because story points can never be used for any kind of work

Because the work's effort is often genuinely unknown in advance, so the estimate ends up being fiction that gets blown through, or the research gets truncated to fit the estimate regardless of whether that's the right stopping point
Because sprints are always exactly two weeks long by definition
Because research questions never take more than a few hours to answer
questions.explain: Unlike a well-understood software ticket, a research question like 'will a sparsity penalty help' doesn't decompose into sub-tasks with known effort, so forcing it into a fixed sprint estimate tends to either be fiction or cut off research at an arbitrary point.

questions.q: What two things does a hypothesis log make visible that a typical task list hides?
options: The researcher's name and the date the task was created
What specific evidence would change the team's mind (the falsification condition) and how much budget is actually left before a decision must be made
The exact git commit hash and config file used
The number of story points assigned to the task
questions.explain: A hypothesis log states a falsifiable claim with its falsification condition and tracks the compute budget spent and remaining against it, surfacing information a generic task list doesn't capture.

questions.q: Why is compute budget often described as a harder timeline constraint than calendar time in research project management?
options: Because calendar time is infinite and therefore never a real constraint
Because a GPU-day spent on one experiment is not available for another, making it a genuinely scarce and non-fungible resource in a way calendar time often isn't
Because compute budget and calendar time are always identical in practice
Because GPUs never run out of capacity in a research setting
questions.explain: GPU-time is directly scarce and exclusive to the experiment consuming it, which ties tracking 'GPU-days spent/remaining' more directly to the actual bottleneck than tracking calendar days against a task.

questions.q: What is a 'time-boxed decision point' in research project management?
options: A deadline imposed without any reference to evidence or experiment results
A pre-committed point, decided before the work starts, specifying what evidence at what point will trigger a decision to continue, pivot, or stop
The exact moment a GPU job finishes running
A meeting scheduled at a fixed weekly cadence regardless of project status
questions.explain: A time-boxed decision point is set in advance, tied to specific evidence (e.g. 'if none of 5 swept values beats the baseline by 1 std by Friday'), and forces an explicit continue/pivot/stop decision rather than leaving it as an unstated intuition.

questions.q: What risk does the lesson say arises from NOT setting an explicit decision point for a research direction?
options: The experiment will automatically stop itself after a fixed number of GPU-days
A direction that isn't working can quietly consume weeks past the point where the evidence already justified stopping, since no checkpoint forces the decision
The team will be legally required to publish a negative result
The compute budget will automatically double
questions.explain: Without a concrete, visible checkpoint, there's nothing forcing a continue/pivot/stop decision, so an unproductive direction can continue consuming time and compute well past where the evidence already pointed to stopping.
